concepts.title: Matter usually exists in one of three everyday states

members.title: Matter usually exists in one of three everyday states
members.content: solid, liquid, and gas. What state matter is in depends on two things: how closely packed its particles are, and how much energy (movement) those particles have.

concepts.title: Particles in matter are arranged differently depending on the state of the substance

members.title: Particles in matter are arranged differently depending on the state of the substance
members.content: Particles in matter are arranged differently depending on the state of the substance. In solids, the particles are tightly packed together in fixed positions, giving the material a definite shape and volume. Liquids have particles that are close together but able to move around, allowing the substance to flow and take the shape of its container. Finally, gases consist of particles that are far apart and moving freely, with no fixed shape or volume.

members.title: As a general rule
members.content: the more energy particles have, the faster they move and the further apart they spread. Solids have the least particle energy and movement; gases have the most.

members.title: Matter
members.content: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. A book, water, air, a spoon, and a balloon all contain matter. Matter can be described using observable properties such as shape, volume, texture, color, and how it behaves inside a container.

members.title: Solid
members.content: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume. Its particles are packed closely together and mainly vibrate in fixed positions. Examples include a stone, pencil, wooden block, and ice cube.

members.title: Solids
members.content: In a solid, particles are packed tightly together in a fixed, orderly pattern. They vibrate in place but do not move past one another.

members.title: Diagram description
members.content:
particles in a solid are drawn as evenly spaced dots arranged in tidy rows and columns, like a grid, showing a fixed, orderly pattern. Key properties of solids Has a fixed shape -- it does not change shape unless a force is applied. Particles are tightly packed and only vibrate in place.
Generally difficult to compress (squeeze into a smaller space).

members.title: Everyday examples
members.content: ice cubes, a wooden chair, a rock, a coin, and a book.

members.title: Liquid
members.content:
A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape. It flows and takes the shape of its container. Its particles are close together but can slide past one another.
Examples include water, milk, and cooking oil.

members.title: Liquids
members.content: In a liquid, particles are still close together, but they have more energy than in a solid. They can slide past one another, which is why liquids can flow and change shape.

members.title: Diagram description (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
particles in a liquid are drawn as dots that are close together but scattered in an irregular, flowing arrangement rather than a neat grid, showing that they can move around each other.
Key properties of liquids Has no fixed shape -- it takes the shape of its container.

members.title: Diagram description (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
Has a fixed volume -- the amount of liquid stays the same even if the container changes.
Particles can slide past each other, allowing the liquid to flow.
Generally difficult to compress, though slightly easier than a solid.

members.title: Everyday examples
members.content: water, milk, cooking oil, and juice.

members.title: Gas
members.content: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume. It spreads out and fills the available space in its container. Its particles are far apart and move freely. Air and water vapor are examples of gases.

members.title: Gases
members.content: In a gas, particles have the most energy of the three states. They move quickly in every direction and spread far apart, filling all the space available to them.

members.title: Diagram description
members.content:
particles in a gas are drawn as widely spaced dots, each with a short line beside it representing fast, free movement in many directions.
Key properties of gases
Has no fixed shape and no fixed volume -- it spreads out to fill its container completely.
Particles move quickly and freely, with large spaces between them.
Easy to compress because there is so much empty space between particles.

members.title: Everyday examples
members.content: the air around you, helium in a balloon, and steam rising from a hot drink.

members.title: Shape
members.content: Solids keep their shape; liquids and gases take the shape of their container.

members.title: Volume
members.content: Solids and liquids have definite volume; gases expand to fill available space.

members.title: Particle arrangement
members.content: Solid particles are tightly packed, liquid particles are close but mobile, and gas particles are widely spaced.

members.title: Flow
members.content: Liquids and gases can flow, while solids normally do not.

members.title: Comparing the Three States
members.content: The table below summarizes the key differences. Row and column headers are labeled with text so the comparison does not depend on color alone.

members.title: 5. Comparing the Three States
members.content: The table compares the properties of solids, liquids, and gases. It shows that solids maintain a fixed shape and volume, with their particles vibrating closely together. Liquids take the shape of their container but maintain a fixed volume, and their particles slide past each other. Finally, gases fill the available space, have a far apart particle spacing, and move quickly and freely.

concepts.title: Changing From One State to Another

members.title: Changing From One State to Another
members.content: Adding or removing heat energy can change matter from one state to another. These changes are called changes of state. The names below describe the direction of each change.

concepts.title: 6. Changing From One State to Another

members.title: 6. Changing From One State to Another
members.content: The figure details the transitions between solid, liquid, and gaseous states of matter. It explains that energy plays a key role in these changes, with adding energy causing a substance to move faster and spread out, as seen in melting and evaporation. Conversely, removing energy causes particles to slow down and lock into place, as demonstrated by freezing and condensation. These processes illustrate how changes in temperature directly influence the state of a substance.

members.title: Everyday Examples
members.content: An ice cube is a solid, melted ice is liquid water, and water vapor is a gas. These examples show that the same substance can exist in different states. Heating and cooling can cause changes of state, but understanding each state should come first.

members.title: Example
members.content: an ice cube (solid) left on a counter absorbs heat from the air. It melts into water (liquid). If that water is heated on a stove until it boils, some of it evaporates into water vapor (gas).

members.title: Everyday Examples
members.content: Water is one of the few substances people commonly see in all three states. The table below lists a few examples for each state.

members.title: 7. Everyday Examples
members.content: This table illustrates how the three states of matter – solid, liquid, and gas – are represented in common everyday materials. It shows that ice, wood, and a metal spoon are all solids, possessing a fixed shape and volume. Similarly, water, cooking oil, and juice are liquids, which have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container. Finally, water vapor or steam, helium, air, and carbon dioxide in soda are all gases, which have no fixed shape or volume and can expand to fill any available space.
